Why the last commit is still needed? Why not to take another lock?

Another idea: could we make systemd-vconsole-setup templated on the console to avoid having to restart it as much? We could keep the non-templated service and only start the templated service from udev for each console that pops up. That should also be more efficient rather than applying the settings to every console for each individual console that pops up.

> Why the last commit is still needed? Why not to take another lock?

With this patch, if `systemctl restart systemd-vconsole-setup` is issued, the previous instance is stopped without error. We *could* do locking, but that'd mean that we'd wait for the previous instance to finish. We want to restart the service at will, for example after updating the configuration, and we don't want to wait for the previous instance to finish. Instead, we want to terminate it and start a new instance that will write the latest font or whatever.

> Another idea: could we make systemd-vconsole-setup templated on the console to avoid having to restart it as much? We could keep the non-templated service and only start the templated service from udev for each console that pops up. That should also be more efficient rather than applying the settings to every console for each individual console that pops up.

Hmm. What you say sounds sensible, but that's not actually what seems to be necessary. Whenever a new vtcon device pops up, we call `systemd-vconsole-setup` without a parameter, which means that it finds a suitable *tty* device (usually `/dev/tty1` or such), calls `setfont` on that device, calls `loadkeys` on that device, and then copies the font and map to other tty devices. I don't think we refer to the actual vtcon device in any way. I don't quite understand why we do this for each vtcon device, but looking at the git history, people reported bugs, e.g. a missing keymap, when we skipped some of the vtcon devices. Doing this for every device sounds bad, but actually there are usually only two, so it's not so bad. I think the most reasonable thing is to merge this as is.

review_comments:
So I don't really get this. In most cases this will lock /dev/tty1, but afaics systemd-firstboot will operate on /dev/console, which are two distinct things.

This code looks like it should explicitly lock /dev/console here, not `fd`.

Or what am I missing? @keszybz?
Does this have to be either-or? Should we just lock both?

ABBA problems loom.

(you'd need to sort them by .st_rdev or so when locking multiple to enforce same lock order, and not deadlock. Not sure if worth the effort)

The goal of the locking was to prevent the tty reset from preventing `setfont` from finishing successfully. My assumption was that if it's operating on e.g. `tty1`, and something else is operating on `console`, those are two different things, and we don't need to serialize. But it's possible that it's wrong.

/dev/console is a weird beast. Different inode, difference device then whatever it "points" to, but all TTY operations get sent to the place it points to... 

Similar is /dev/tty0, which is also such a weird beast and forwards all TTY operations to the foreground tty /dev/tty1, /dev/tty2, …

So basically, there's a very common case where you have three distinct TTY inodes that actually can be used interchangably pretty much. If we execute an op on one of them, we need to take that into consideration and adjust our locking regime accordingly.

One simple way out: just ignore anything fine grained, and add a big lock on /dev/console, ignore the other ttys. That way you are always right, and don't have to deal with races around /dev/console and /dev/tty0 changing meaning half-way.
